Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 72, verses 1–2:

As for hearing of perception (samaa' al-idrak), it is in His saying, relating the words of the believing jinn: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, (1) guiding to right conduct, so we have believed in it.﴾

And His saying: ﴿O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], the verse.

This is hearing of perception to which belief and response were joined.

(Section: On the eighteenth class: the class of the jinn)

The Muslims agree that among them are the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked. Allah the Exalted said, reporting about them: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those beneath that; we were in divided ways﴾ [al-Jinn: 11].

Mujahid said: they mean Muslims and disbelievers.

The Muslims agree that the disbelieving jinn are in the Fire, and the Qur'an has indicated this in more than one place, such as His saying: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13].

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179].

In sum, this is a matter known necessarily from the religion of Islam, and it entails that the jinn are obligated by the laws of the prophets and must follow them. The Muslims agree that Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to the jinn and mankind, and that it is obligatory upon the jinn to obey him just as it is obligatory upon mankind.

As for the ruling on their believers in the Hereafter, the majority of the early generations (al-Salaf) and the later ones (al-Khalaf) hold that they are in Paradise. Al-Bukhari (rahimahu Allah) gave a chapter heading to this in his Sahih, saying: "Chapter: The reward of the jinn and their punishment, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses?﴾ [al-An'am: 130]."

These are the positions of people regarding their rulings in the Hereafter.

As for their rulings in this world, people have differed over whether they are responsible (mukallaf) for the commands and prohibitions or not.

The correct view, held by the majority of the people of Islam, is that they are commanded, prohibited, and obligated by the Islamic Shari'ah, and the evidences from the Qur'an and the Sunnah for this are more than can be counted. Among what indicates their obligation is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when We turned toward you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an, and when they attended it, they said, "Be silent." And when it was concluded, they went back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29–32]. This indicates their obligation in several respects:

1. That Allah, glory be to Him, turned them toward His Messenger to listen to the Qur'an so that they would believe in it, comply with its commands, and refrain from its prohibitions.

2. That they returned to their people as warners, and warning is informing of fear after its causes have been established. So it is known that they warned their people of the Fire if they disobeyed the Messenger.

3. That they reported that they had heard the Qur'an, understood it, and comprehended it. This indicates their capacity for the knowledge by which the proof is established, and that they are able to carry out what is in it. Obligation entails only knowledge and ability.

4. That they said to their people: ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him﴾. This is explicit that they are obligated and commanded to respond to the Messenger, and that response means affirming what he reports and obeying what he commands.

5. That they said: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾, and forgiveness occurs only for a sin, which is opposing a command.

6. That they said: ﴿And protect you from a painful punishment﴾. This indicates that whoever among them does not respond to the caller of Allah will not be protected from the painful punishment, and this is explicit in the Islamic Shari'ah's binding them.

7. That they said: ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape within the earth, and he will have no protectors other than Him﴾. This is a severe threat to whoever among them lags behind the caller of Allah.

It is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to them, and that they asked him for provisions for themselves and their animals. So he made for them every bone over which the name of Allah had been mentioned, and every dropping as fodder for their animals, and he forbade us from cleaning ourselves with them (1). Even if there were nothing in this except His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15], it would suffice; and He has informed that He punishes the disbelieving jinn, which is sufficient proof that they are obligated to follow the messengers.

When their obligation to the laws of the prophets, their being held accountable for them, and their gathering on the Day of Resurrection for reward and punishment are known, it is known that their righteous ones are in Paradise just as their evildoers are in the Fire.

And when their obligation is established, with their division into Muslims, disbelievers, righteous ones, and those beneath that, as contained in Surah al-Jinn, then they are in the reckoning in the manner of the human classes mentioned earlier, except that there is no messenger among them, but rather warners. Their highest rank is the rank of the righteous. And had they a higher rank than it, they would have mentioned it. The Qur'an has indicated their division into three categories: righteous, those beneath them, and disbelievers. Mankind is distinguished above them by the rank of messengership and prophethood, and the rank of those brought near (to Allah). And Allah knows best.

This is what the enumeration has reached regarding the classes of the responsible beings in the Hereafter, and they are eighteen classes. Each class has a highest, a lowest, and a middle level, and they are degrees before Allah. Allah the Exalted gathers each like with its like and each equal with its equal, and joins them in the same degree. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

(Preference of mankind over the jinn)

As for His words: ﴿And we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against God﴾

The secret of this is known from the context, for this is a recounting of the words of the believing jinn when they heard the Qur'an, as God the Exalted says: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened, and they said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an…﴾ and the verses that follow.

The Qur'an was first addressed to mankind and was sent down to their Prophet, and they were the first to affirm and to deny, before the jinn. So the words of the believing jinn, ﴿And we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against God﴾, came with mankind placed first, because of their precedence in being addressed by the Qur'an and their precedence in affirmation and denial.

Another benefit is that this is a recounting of the words of the believing jinn to their people after they returned to them and informed them of what they had heard of the Qur'an, its greatness, and its guidance to right conduct.

Then they offered an excuse for what they had believed at first, contrary to what they had heard of right guidance: that they had not thought that mankind and the jinn would speak a lie against God.

So their mention of mankind first here is more effective in calling to the truth, and more eloquent in clearing them of accusation.

For they had opposed what they used to hear from mankind and the jinn once their falsehood became clear to them. So beginning with mention of mankind is more eloquent in negating the purpose and the accusation, and so that their people would not think they had sided with mankind against them, since they were the first to acknowledge that they had fabricated lies against God the Exalted.

This is among the most subtle and profound meanings, and whoever reflects on its placement in the discourse will know its soundness.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 72, verse 6:

The one who is sought for refuge is Allah alone, the Lord of the daybreak, the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, the God of mankind, to whom alone it is fitting to seek refuge, and no one of His creation is to be sought for refuge. Rather, He is the One who grants safety to those who seek refuge, protects them, and keeps them from the evil of that from which they seek refuge.

Allah the Exalted has informed in His Book about those who sought refuge in His creation, that their seeking refuge increased them in transgression and burden, saying, relating about the believing jinn: ﴿And that there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn, so they increased them in burden﴾.

It is stated in the tafsir that a man from the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah, when he traveled and was overtaken by night in a desolate land, would say: "I seek refuge with the chief of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people."

So he would spend the night in security and protection from them until morning.

That is, the humans increased the jinn by their seeking refuge with their chiefs in burden, meaning in transgression, sin, and evil.

They would say: "We have made the humans and the jinn subservient." Al-rahq (burden) in the speech of the Arabs means sin and the violation of what is forbidden.

So by this seeking of refuge they increased them in committing what was forbidden of arrogance and self-exaltation, so they thought that they had become masters over the humans and the jinn.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 72, verse 11:

Mujahid said: "They mean Muslims and disbelievers."

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: "Your kinds (amthalakum). Among them are the Qadariyya, the Murji'a and the Rafida."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Diverse colours (alwanan shatta)."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Sects (shi'a) and factions (firaq)."

The meaning of the statement is: different categories and scattered schools of thought.

Then it has been said regarding the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the verse: ﴿And among us are some who are other than that﴾, meaning: "and among us are a people other than that," so the qualified noun (al-mawsuf) was omitted and its qualifying adjective (al-sifa) was placed in its position,

like His saying: ﴿There is none among us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: "none among us but he who has a known station."

And like His saying: ﴿And among those who are Jews are listeners to falsehood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], meaning: "a group of listeners to falsehood."

And like His saying: ﴿Among those who are Jews are those who distort words from their places﴾ [al-Nisa': 46], meaning: "a group who distort."

And like His saying, according to the more apparent of the two opinions: ﴿And among those who associate others with Allah is one who wishes that he could live a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96], meaning: "a group, one of whom wishes."

And the poet said:

﴿They remained, and among them was one whose tears ran ahead, and another who held back the tear of the eye with the drops of sorrow⦌

Meaning: "and among them was one whose tears..."

As for their saying: ﴿We were of diverse ways, separate paths﴾, it is an explanation of their saying: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those who are other than that﴾. Meaning: we were people of diverse ways, the ways being the schools of thought; its singular is ṭarīqa, which is a school of thought. The word qidad is the plural of qiddah, like qit'ah and qiṭa' in form and meaning. It derives from al-qadd, which means cutting.

It has also been said: in the diversity of our conditions we were like the diverse paths in their diversity.

According to this view, the meaning is "we were diverse paths, separate," and this is not a strong interpretation.

Weaker than it is the view of those who said that ṭarā'iq is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning "we were in diverse roads," like the saying: "The fox has smoothed the road."

This is not a reading that the most eloquent speech would bear.

It has also been said: the meaning is "our paths were diverse paths," so the genitive-possessor was omitted and the possessed noun was placed in its position.

(Section)

Since it is known that the jinn are charged with the laws of the prophets, are held accountable for them, and will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection for reward and punishment, it follows that their good-doers are in Paradise just as their wrong-doers are in the Fire. This is indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted, relating of their believers: ﴿And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it. So whoever believes in his Lord will not fear injustice or burden﴾ [al-Jinn: 13]. By this argument al-Bukhari also argued.

The way of argument from it is that the "bakhs" (diminishing) that is negated is the reduction of reward, and the "rahq" (burden) is the increase in punishment beyond what one has done. So his good deeds will not be diminished, nor will his evil deeds be increased.

A parallel to this is the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, will not fear injustice or diminution﴾ [Ta-Ha: 112].

That is, he will not fear an increase in his evil deeds nor a decrease in his good deeds.

And the Almighty said, reporting about them: ﴿And among us are those who submit [to Allah], and among us are those who deviate [from the truth]﴾

So the Muslims, those who believed in Allah and His Messenger, are among them, and the qasitun, those who are unjust and deviate from the truth, are among them. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are those who set up rivals to Allah. It is said: aqsaṭa al-rajul when he acts justly, so he is muqsit. Among its usage is: ﴿And act justly; indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

And qasaṭa when he acts unjustly, so he is qasit.

﴿And as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15].

These verses include their division into three categories: the righteous, those below the righteous, and disbelievers.

These categories correspond to the categories of the children of Adam, which are also three: the righteous (abrar), the moderate (muqtasidun), and the disbelievers.

So the ṣāliḥūn correspond to the abrar, those below them correspond to the muqtasidun, and the qasitun correspond to the disbelievers. This is like the division the Exalted made of the Children of Israel into these three categories in His saying: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into communities; among them are the righteous, and among them are others than that﴾ [al-A'raf: 168].

Those among them who were saved are those who are excluded from the mention of the wrongdoers, and they are the evil successors who came after them. And since mankind is more complete than the jinn and more perfect in intellect, they were given three additional categories that the jinn do not have: the Messengers, the Prophets, and the muqarrabun (those brought near).

So there is no category of these among the jinn; rather, their attainable station is righteousness.

Some eccentric people went so far as to claim that there are Messengers and Prophets among them, citing His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], and His saying: ﴿And when We turned toward you a company of the jinn...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners﴾ [al-Nisa': 165].

This is an anomalous view that is not to be given weight, and it is not known from the early generation of the Companions, the Successors, and the Imams of Islam.

His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130] does not indicate that the messengers came from each of the two groups. Rather, since the messengers were from mankind, and the jinn were commanded to follow them, it is correct to say to mankind and jinn: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you?"

A parallel to this is saying to the Arabs and non-Arabs: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you, O assembly of Arabs and non-Arabs?" This does not require that there be messengers from each of these groups.

And the Exalted said: ﴿And made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], and there is not a moon in every heaven.

And His saying: ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. Warning is more general than messengership, and the more general does not necessitate the more specific. The Exalted said: ﴿Why did not a group from every division of them go forth, so that they might gain understanding in religion and warn their people when they return to them?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122].

So these are warners, and they are not messengers.

Many of the early generation said: the Messengers are from mankind, while among the jinn there are warners. The Exalted said: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the cities﴾ [Yusuf: 109].

This indicates that He did not send a jinn, nor a woman, nor a Bedouin.

As for the Exalted calling the jinn "men" in His saying: ﴿And that there were men from mankind who sought refuge in men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6],

the term "men" is not applied to them absolutely; rather, it is a designation restricted by His saying ﴿from the jinn﴾. So they are men of the jinn, and that does not necessitate their inclusion among "men" when used without qualification, just as you say: "men of stone," "men of wood," and the like.

The Siddiq of this community and its most steadfast man, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about istiqamah (steadfastness). He said: "That you do not associate anything with Allah." He meant steadfastness upon pure tawhid (monotheism).

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Istiqamah is that you remain steadfast in obeying the commands and avoiding the prohibitions, and that you do not swerve away like the swerving of foxes."

Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding *istaqamu* (﻿استقاموا): "Sincerely devoting the deed to Allah."

Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said regarding *istaqamu*: "Fulfilling the obligatory duties."

Al-Hasan said: "They remained steadfast upon the command of Allah, so they acted in His obedience and avoided His disobedience."

Mujahid said: "They remained steadfast upon the testimony that there is no god but Allah, until they met Allah."

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul, say: "They remained steadfast in His love and His worship, so they did not turn away from Him to the right or to the left."

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Sufyan ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I said:

"O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying about Islam about which I will not ask anyone other than you."

He said: "Say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast."

The reality of worship (al-ta'abbud) is humility and submission toward the Beloved. From this comes their saying, "a paved road" (tariq mu'abbad), meaning one that has been made smooth, its surface worn down by feet. Thus the servant ('abd) is the one whom love and submission to his Beloved have tamed. For this reason, the most noble of the servant's states and stations is servanthood ('ubudiyyah, the state of being a devoted servant), and he has no station more noble than it.

Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the most honored of creation before Him and the most beloved of them to Him, His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), by his servanthood in his noblest stations: the station of calling to Him, the station of challenging with prophethood, and the station of the Night Journey. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him, they almost became a crowd pressing upon him.﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]

And He said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]

And He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa.﴾ [al-Isra': 1]

The hadith of intercession: "Go to Muhammad, a servant whom Allah has forgiven his earlier and later sins."

He attained the station of intercession through the perfection of his servanthood and the perfection of Allah's forgiveness of him. Allah, glorified is He, created creation to worship Him alone, with no partner, which is the most perfect kind of love together with the most perfect kind of submission. This is the reality of Islam (submission to Allah) and the creed (millah) of Ibrahim (Abraham), and whoever turns away from it has made a fool of his own soul.

(Fa'idah)

Guidance (rushd) is sometimes contrasted with harm (ḍarr) and evil (sharr). God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say: Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or any guidance﴾ [al-Jinn: 21].

And the believing jinn said: ﴿And indeed, we do not know whether evil is intended for those upon the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn: 10].

So guidance (rushd) is the opposite of error (ghayy), as in His saying: ﴿And if they see the way of guidance (al-rushd), they will not take it as a way; but if they see the way of error (al-ghayy), they will take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146].

It is also contrasted with harm and evil, as has preceded, because error (ghayy) is the cause of harm and evil occurring and befalling its possessor. Thus harm and evil are the ultimate outcome and fruit of error (al-baghy), just as mercy and success (al-falah) are the ultimate outcome and fruit of guidance (al-huda).
